newsitem.title: CANADA: Recent Canada natgas prices seen as sustainable.
newsitem.headline: Recent Canada natgas prices seen as sustainable.

text.p: With a recent sharp rise in spot-market prices, industry experts are seeing signs that the dog days of Canadian natural gas could be drawing to a close.

In the past week, a quick jump in the price of gas for export to California and the U.S. Pacific Northwest has surprised market players, who have suffered under the weight of North America's most depressed gas market for a year and a half.
Only last winter's bone-chilling cold offered producers brief respite.
Alberta spot market prices have also climbed about 15 cents in the past two weeks, mostly to feed the western U.S. demand, traders have said.

"As far as the Alberta price, at about C$1.43 (per gigajoule), I think that's sustainable for the next couple of months," said Brent Friedenburg of Calgary-based Friedenburg & Associates. "I know that winter gas, the November to March period, on the spot market is in the C$1.38-C$1.40 range."

Prices at Sumas, Washington, where gas is transferred to Northwest Pipeline in the U.S. from Westcoast Energy Inc's British Columbia system, were quoted on Wednesday as high as US$1.96 per million British thermal units, up 64 cents from the week before.
The prices were point's highest since February 1994.
Western Canadian gas prices for about 18 months have severely lagged those in the eastern Canada and the U.S., even when the price of transportation is factored in.
The low prices have often been blamed on a scarcity of export pipeline space, which forces Canadian producers to compete with each other within the borders of Alberta and B.C.
Numerous pipeline expansion proposals valued at several billion dollars are currently being considered, but none would be on stream before 1998.

The current price runup is thanks to high demand in California and the Pacific Northwest, where cooler weather has been predicted, forcing utilities to use gas to generate incremental electricity, players have said.
Spot gas prices for gas in the San Juan Basin in the Southwest U.S., Canada's main competitor for supply to the region, have also jumped in the past week.
"All of a sudden they start looking at what the fuel oil prices are doing and they become worried," said Martin Molyneaux, analyst with FirstEnergy Capital Corp. "The demand for gas increases."
Prices at Kingsgate, B.C., where Alberta gas enters the Pacific Gas Transmission pipeline to California, have also jumped in the past week and pushed the line's capacity use to over 85-percent.

Gas at the AECO storage hub in Alberta, the province's main pricing center, has climbed steadily since the end of summer, most recently due to the western demand and difficulty NOVA Gas Transmission Ltd's intra-Alberta pipeline system has had keeping loads balanced.

Several marketers said this week that, while they were surprised by how quickly gas supplies tightened and prices rose, the current levels in western North America may have reached an equilibrium after over a year of deep discounts. Analysts said they agreed.

"If you look at the East Coast-West Coast differential, Henry Hub versus California State border, we're within two or three cents plus or minus," Molyneaux said. "We haven't been at that kind of tolerance level since September '95."

He said it was likely that his firm's estimate for a 1997 corporate weighted price average in Canada of C$1.75 per thousand cubic feet would be met, especially if this winter is normally cold. -- Reuters Calgary Bureau 403 531-1624
